title: The State of Childhood in the U.S.
author: Institute for Family Studies
summary: A new Institute for Family Studies survey of nearly 24,000 U.S. parents covering over 40,000 children confirms that Jonathan Haidt's central observation from The Anxious Generation remains widely true: American kids are still overprotected in the real world and underprotected in the virtual world. Average weekly online device time grows from 4.5 hours at age 3 to nearly 20 hours at age 17, with parental controls that are surprisingly lax: fewer than 20% of teenagers who use smartphones have content filters, and by age 3, under half of tablet-using preschoolers have time limits. Physical freedom is even more restricted: by age 14, a majority of American kids are not allowed to travel beyond their own street, and even at 17 over 60% cannot leave their neighborhoods unsupervised. Walkability of neighborhood has zero correlation with how much outdoor freedom children have. The class-based finding inverts the traditional digital divide: parents with graduate degrees are more likely to implement screen-time limits (59%) than parents with only a high school diploma (40%), and less-educated parents are more likely to give their children smartphones by age 9-14. A clear sign of privilege today is the ability to establish boundaries around screen access and encourage free outdoor play.
points: * American kids remain overprotected in the real world and underprotected online: 4.5 weekly device hours at age 3, nearly 20 at age 17, while by age 14 a majority cannot travel beyond their own street. * Parental controls are lax across all ages: under 20% of 17-year-olds with smartphones have content filters; most preschoolers with tablets have no time limits or parental codes required. * By age 17, 90% of children have a smartphone, 60% have a gaming console -- yet 60%+ cannot leave their neighborhoods unsupervised. * Walkability and neighborhood characteristics have zero correlation with children's autonomous mobility or outdoor play time -- the restrictions are cultural, not environmental. * The traditional digital divide is now inverted: graduate-degree parents are the most likely to limit screen time and the least likely to give smartphones to 9-14 year olds -- privilege today means less screen access, not more.
quotes: overprotection in the real world and underprotection in the virtual world -- remains widely true for most children and teens.
By the age of 11, smartphones become the primary medium for internet access among American kids, with over 60% having a smartphone.
Even by 17-years-old, about 60% of American kids are still not allowed to leave their neighborhood unsupervised.
Parents with a graduate degree are more likely to establish screen time limits or phone drop-off rules for children over age 10 than less-educated parents.
in any given week, the differences are modest. But over time, they compound, becoming extremely meaningful.
The physical form of a neighborhood has no correlation at all with how much autonomy kids have to go places or how much time they play outside.
a clear sign of privilege today is the ability of parents to both establish boundaries around their children that limit their access to screens, and encourage them to freely play.
